scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Follow-up summary queries to the coordinator take 40+ seconds. It spawns a synthesis subagent each time, passing 80K tokens. But the coordinator already has these findings in its context. Best fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Handle summarization DIRECTLY at the coordinator level.
The coordinator already has the findings — spawning a subagent is the anti-pattern.

Subagents start with ZERO knowledge and cannot inherit coordinator context.
Spawning one and passing 80K tokens = unnecessary latency + wasteful token transfer.

❌ Compress then pass (still spawns unnecessarily)
❌ Increase subagent context window (bottleneck is spawn + transfer, not limit)
❌ Cache subagent responses (band-aid, doesn't fix architectural flaw)
❌ fork_session (for divergent exploration, not latency optimization)

💡 If the coordinator already has the information, use it directly.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: After web search and document analysis finish, the coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent. How should findings be passed to it?
scenario.ba:
✅ Pass COMPLETE findings directly embedded in the synthesis subagent's prompt
using a STRUCTURED format separating content from metadata:

{ claim, evidence_excerpt, source_url, document_name, publication_date }

❌ Let synthesis call search tools itself (violates scope separation)
❌ Let synthesis read coordinator's session history (impossible — isolated)
❌ Pass prose summary only (loses source attribution — can't cite)

💡 Structured format preserves both content AND metadata for downstream attribution.
💡 Subagents cannot inherit context — explicitly inject everything.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: The coordinator gives a web search subagent a 40-step procedural checklist. On emerging topics it reports 'insufficient results' instead of trying alternatives. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Replace procedural instructions with GOAL-ORIENTED prompts:
→ Specify research goals + quality criteria
   (e.g., 'minimum 5 distinct claims from credible sources')
→ Grants the subagent authority to adapt its approach

❌ More steps in the checklist (compounds rigidity — more steps = more to fail)
❌ Expand query lists (can't hard-code for unknown/emerging patterns)
❌ Generic single-word queries (degrades research specificity)

💡 Procedural checklist = rigid executor. Goal-oriented = adaptive agent.
💡 When pre-specified paths fail, goals let the agent find alternatives.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Document analysis subagent processes 12 legal citations SEQUENTIALLY — takes 3+ minutes. How do you reduce latency?
scenario.ba:
✅ Emit ALL 12 Task tool calls in a SINGLE coordinator response turn.
SDK runs them CONCURRENTLY.
Total time = duration of the LONGEST single task (~15–20s vs 3+ min).

❌ Increase context window (doesn't address sequential architecture)
❌ fork_session (for divergent exploration, not pipeline parallelism)
❌ Message Batches API (up to 24-hour SLA — catastrophically worse for this)

💡 Sequential processing of independent parallel tasks = classic anti-pattern.
💡 Multiple Task calls in ONE response = concurrent execution by the SDK.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Agent has 50+ connector tools. Frequently selects the wrong one even when explicitly instructed to search first. Most effective architectural fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Add a search_connectors tool that DYNAMICALLY SCOPES the toolset.
Agent calls search_connectors → system injects only 2–3 matched connectors for the next turn.

Reduces decision complexity from 50+ choices to 2–3 choices.

❌ Rewrite all 50 descriptions (50+ active tools still cause overload)
❌ Monolithic API (removes model's ability to distinguish between variants)
❌ Better error handling (reactive band-aid — scoping prevents the error)

💡 Dynamic scoping: proactive prevention beats reactive correction.
💡 Decision complexity with 50+ tools overwhelms even perfect descriptions.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Agent queries internal databases but users say 'research database' instead of the exact system name 'db_res_01'. How to make this reliable?
scenario.ba:
✅ Use an ENUM parameter explicitly listing the allowed database system names.
Model maps user's natural language to exact backend values BEFORE execution.
Constraint enforced at the schema level — before the tool runs.

❌ Freeform string + fuzzy backend matching (pushes ambiguity downstream, unpredictable)
❌ Reject invalid names at runtime (wastes a full execution turn)
❌ Search all databases simultaneously (spikes cost, latency, context bloat)

💡 Enums constrain LLM output to valid values deterministically.
💡 Model's semantic understanding maps 'research DB' → 'db_res_01' reliably.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Multiple shipping carriers return timestamps/statuses in completely different JSON formats. How should you design tool output?
scenario.ba:
✅ NORMALIZE carrier responses into a single COMMON SCHEMA before returning to agent.
e.g., { status, estimated_delivery, carrier_name, tracking_id }
Vendor quirks are abstracted in middleware — the agent sees clean, consistent data.

❌ Pass raw JSON + prompt instructions for parsing (brittle; burns attention on format)
❌ Separate tools per carrier (bloats the toolset unnecessarily)
❌ Return raw + normalized (adds noise, wastes context on data agent doesn't need)

💡 Agents reason best over consistent, predictable data structures.
💡 Normalize BEFORE the agent sees it — not after.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Agent chains get_property_details() → gets address → passes to get_neighborhood_info(address). 2-step chain adds latency and failure points. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Modify get_neighborhood_info to accept property_id DIRECTLY and resolve address INTERNALLY.
Internalizes the predictable mechanical ID-to-string lookup.
Reduces agent turns and removes a brittle inter-step failure point.

❌ Merge into one get_all_property_data (over-consolidates distinct capabilities)
❌ Improve the prompt (doesn't fix the architectural latency)
❌ Middle-tier helper tool (adds surface area, preserves the chaining problem)

💡 Internalize predictable dependencies into tool logic — don't make the LLM do them.
💡 If the chaining is always the same and always required, it belongs inside the tool.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: update_game_score(date, team_name) frequently fails due to ambiguous nicknames and rematches on the same day. Most reliable architectural fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Introduce a search_games tool that returns a game_id.
Update the scoring tool to accept ONLY the game_id.

Separates DISCOVERY (finding the right game) from ACTION (updating its score).
Machine-usable IDs = no ambiguity.

❌ Strict ISO-8601 date + official team names (doesn't solve rematches on same day)
❌ Better tool descriptions (doesn't eliminate inherent NL ambiguity)
❌ Regex validation (catches format errors but doesn't resolve the correct game)

💡 Replace tools relying on ambiguous human-entered text with a lookup/action pattern.
💡 Rule: if two items have the same human-readable attributes, use an ID.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Agent processes employee reimbursements. Policy: payouts > $500 CANNOT be automatically disbursed — must go to pending approval. Where must this rule be enforced?
scenario.ba:
✅ INSIDE the process_reimbursement tool logic itself (deterministic enforcement).
Even if the agent hallucinates or is prompt-injected,
payloads over $500 will always degrade to 'pending approval'.

❌ requires_approval boolean the agent sets (agent could hallucinate false)
❌ Strict system prompt instruction (probabilistic — non-zero failure rate)
❌ Two separate tools + trust agent to pick (agent selection can fail)

💡 If a rule CANNOT be bypassed → backend enforcement, not prompt.
💡 This is the canonical 'hooks vs prompts' example at the tool level.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: An MCP server exposes content catalogs, issue hierarchies, and schemas. Agents waste time making sequential lookup calls just to discover what data exists. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Expose each MCP server's content catalog as an MCP RESOURCE.
Agents can read what data exists BEFORE deciding which tool calls to make.
Eliminates exploratory 'what's in here?' spam.

❌ Consolidate all MCP servers into one giant endpoint (destroys microservice boundaries)
❌ Add a discover_data tool to every server (re-invents what Resources already do natively)
❌ Keyword routing at coordinator (brittle when questions span multiple systems)

💡 MCP Resources = lightweight context. MCP Tools = execution.
💡 Agents should be able to 'see the map' before 'taking the journey'.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: New developer joins the team. Claude Code doesn't apply project conventions. Team lead stored all conventions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on their own machine. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Move conventions to .claude/CLAUDE.md at the PROJECT ROOT, committed to git.
Automatically available to everyone who clones the repo — no manual steps.

❌ Have new hire copy the lead's CLAUDE.md (manual, error-prone, doesn't scale)
❌ Put in README.md (Claude doesn't auto-discover README files)
❌ Set ANTHROPIC_CLAUDE_PATH env var (this env variable doesn't exist)

💡 ~/.claude/ = user-level = personal = NOT version-controlled
💡 .claude/ at project root = project-level = team-wide = git-tracked

Diagnose: /memory command shows which files are actually loaded.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: PR review workflow: every PR must be reviewed for code style, security vulnerabilities, AND documentation accuracy. Which architectural pattern?
scenario.ba:
✅ PROMPT CHAINING: separate sequential passes, each with a distinct focus.
1. Style pass: only evaluate code formatting and conventions
2. Security pass: only look for vulnerability patterns
3. Documentation pass: only verify accuracy of comments and docs
Merge outputs into final synthesis.

❌ Dynamic subagent decomposition (the workflow is predictable and ALWAYS the same)
❌ A routing agent (all 3 aspects are needed for EVERY PR, not just one)
❌ Single massive prompt covering all 3 simultaneously (attention dilution across concerns)

💡 When workflow is highly predictable and mandatory: prompt chaining.
💡 Isolating distinct cognitive lenses prevents cross-contamination.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: You're restructuring a monolith into 40+ microservices — changes across dozens of files, decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Best approach?
scenario.ba:
✅ PLAN MODE: Explore codebase, understand dependencies, design approach BEFORE making changes.
→ Safe exploration + architectural design with zero side effects
→ User reviews and approves the plan before any changes happen
→ Then direct execution for the approved implementation

❌ Start with direct execution and make incremental changes
   (risks costly rework when dependency conflicts discovered late)
❌ Direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions
   (assumes you know the structure without exploring it first)

💡 Large-scale + architectural decisions → plan mode first, always.
💡 The cost of a planning pass is trivial vs. the cost of reversing wrong changes.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Invoice extraction: extracted line items don't sum to the stated total. Best architectural approach?
scenario.ba:
✅ Extract BOTH stated_total AND calculated_total.
Compare them. Flag mismatches with conflict_detected: true for human review.

JSON schema prevents SYNTAX errors.
Self-correction patterns handle SEMANTIC errors (bad math).

❌ Adjust line items to match total (FABRICATES data — corrupts integrity)
❌ Secondary LLM reconciliation step (unnecessary overhead when deterministic check works)
❌ More few-shot math examples (cannot guarantee arithmetic deterministically)

💡 Downstream code handles discrepancy explicitly rather than silently 'fixing' source.
💡 Honest conflict flag > silent incorrect data every time.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Processing 50K documents. Initial 500-doc test shows 18% need 2–3 prompt refinements. Most cost-efficient strategy?
scenario.ba:
✅ Refine prompt on representative SAMPLE to maximize first-pass success.
THEN batch-process all 50K documents.

Iterative resubmissions at scale destroy Batch API cost savings.
Fix the failure modes on 500 docs — then batch.

❌ Batch all 50K immediately (expensive cycles of large-batch resubmission)
❌ Sync API for all 50K (loses the 50% cost savings)
❌ Incremental 5K batches (still pays for failure learning at near-production scale)

💡 Refine → stabilize → batch. Order matters enormously for cost.
💡 18% failure at 50K = 9,000 resubmissions if not fixed first.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: SLA requires results within 30 hours. Batch API takes up to 24h. Which submission frequency meets SLA while maximizing cost efficiency?
scenario.ba:
✅ Every 6 HOURS — the maximum interval that still satisfies the SLA.

Math: batch_interval + 24h ≤ 30h → interval ≤ 6h
6h = fewest submissions = lowest overhead = maximum cost efficiency.
It sits precisely on the optimal boundary.

❌ Every 4h: meets SLA but submits more batches than necessary (extra overhead)
❌ Once daily: 24 + 24 = 48h → FAILS the 30h SLA
❌ Sync API: loses 50% cost savings

⚠️ Exam asks for MAX COST EFFICIENCY → 6h is correct (on the boundary)
⚠️ Production reality: use 4h buffer. Exam: 6h.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Pipeline uses extract_metadata (returns DOI) + enrichment tools that REQUIRE a DOI first. Model sometimes calls enrichment first, which fails. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Set tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"} on TURN 1.
Then switch to tool_choice: "auto" for subsequent turns.
DOI is now in context → enrichment tools function correctly.

❌ Prompt instruction "always call extract_metadata first" (non-zero failure rate)
❌ Merge all tools into one (decreases composability, massively bloats complexity)
❌ "auto" + restrict enrichment descriptions (model may still call them in same turn)

💡 When deterministic execution order matters → deterministic API constraint.
💡 Probabilistic prompt guidance never guarantees execution order.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Technical manual lists two conflicting battery capacities — body text says one value, specs table says another (historically 90% correct). How should the schema handle this?
scenario.ba:
✅ Change the field to capture ALL conflicting values WITH their source locations.
Preserve provenance for downstream reconciliation.
Don't force premature collapse into a single value.

❌ Halt and flag for manual correction before extraction (impractical at scale)
❌ Single-value schema + prompt to pick most likely (destroys conflict evidence)
❌ Hard-code 'always use specs table' (locks in a guaranteed 10% error rate)

💡 Even at 90% reliability, hardcoding guarantees 10% wrong data.
💡 Preserve conflict structurally — let downstream logic with full context decide.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Multi-agent pipeline crashes after completing 12 of 18 documents. How to resume without losing fidelity or repeating completed work?
scenario.ba:
✅ Extract completed work to a STRUCTURED JSON CHECKPOINT file.
Start a FRESH session.
Inject checkpoint at top of the prompt:
• complete: [list of finished docs]
• partial: [partially processed with sections complete]
• pending: [not yet started]

❌ --resume directly on crashed session (stale tool results → unreliable reasoning)
❌ fork_session (for divergent exploration, NOT crash recovery)
❌ Resume without marking partial states (agent re-does or skips work)

💡 Stale tool results from a crashed session are untrustworthy.
💡 Checkpoint → fresh session → inject → resume from verified good state.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: 2024 web search stats vs. 2021 document analysis stats get flagged as 'contradictory' by the synthesis agent. Single best fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Require publication_date in structured subagent outputs.
Update synthesis agent instructions:
→ Differing values across DISTINCT dates = temporal progression, not conflict
→ conflict_detected: true ONLY for same time period with different values

With dates: { value: '$35B', date: '2021' } and { value: '$50B', date: '2024' }
→ Synthesis correctly identifies a GROWTH TREND, not a contradiction

❌ Pick most recent value (misses the temporal analysis entirely)
❌ Average the values (fabricates a number neither source supports)

💡 Temporal metadata prevents chronological growth from being misread as conflict.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: 10K batch completes. 300 docs (3%) fail with context_length_exceeded. Most cost-effective fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Extract ONLY the 300 failed documents using their custom_id.
CHUNK them into smaller segments.
Resubmit ONLY the failures as a new batch.

❌ Resubmit all 10K with smaller chunk size
   (pays for 9,700 already-successful documents — massive waste)
❌ Switch the 300 to sync API (2x cost; no latency benefit for docs requiring chunking)
❌ Increase context window limit globally (fixed model constraint — not configurable)

💡 custom_id maps each request to its response. Isolation of failures is trivial.
💡 Resubmitting only failures = preserving the Batch API cost advantage.

scenario.fr: SCENARIO: Synthesis agent passes prose summary → report agent can't attribute claims because source metadata was lost during summarization. Fix?
scenario.ba:
✅ Assign citation_id at the EARLIEST source discovery stage.
Require synthesis agent to produce:
  (a) narrative with inline [src_001] references AND
  (b) separate structured citation index: { id, url, source, date, key_quote }

❌ Re-include full source text in summary (context bloat → lost in middle failures)
❌ Report agent infers sources from claims (hallucinates plausible-sounding citations)
❌ Prompt synthesis to 'preserve sources' in prose
   (probabilistic — drops under token pressure; not structural)

💡 Separate content from metadata STRUCTURALLY.
💡 Never rely on prose summaries to preserve both simultaneously.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Add few-shot examples to enforce TOOL ORDERING'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Tool ordering is a COMPLIANCE concern, not a demonstration concern.
Few-shot examples influence behavior probabilistically — never deterministically.

✅ CORRECT: Programmatic prerequisites / forced tool_choice
• Block process_refund until get_customer returns verified customer ID
• tool_choice: {type:'tool', name:'extract_metadata'} on first turn
• PreToolUse hook that checks prerequisite state

💡 Compliance-critical ordering = deterministic API constraints.
💡 Few-shot examples for ordering = hoping the model 'gets it.'
   With financial consequences on the line, hope is not an architecture.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Route escalations based on self-reported confidence scores'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

LLM self-reported confidence is POORLY CALIBRATED.
The model is confidently WRONG on the hard cases that most need routing.

Correct calibration:
• Collect model confidence scores on LABELED VALIDATION DATA
• Measure ACTUAL accuracy vs. reported confidence
• Set thresholds EMPIRICALLY
• Recalibrate on every prompt or model change

✅ CORRECT escalation triggers:
• Customer explicitly requests a human
• Policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific situation
• Agent cannot make meaningful progress

💡 Don't ask the model how confident it is. Measure it empirically.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Switch all workflows to Batch API for 50% cost savings'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Batch API has NO guaranteed SLA — up to 24-hour window.
This makes it UNSUITABLE for any BLOCKING workflow.

Blocking workflows that MUST use real-time API:
• Pre-merge PR checks (developer is waiting)
• Live customer interactions
• Any workflow where a human blocks on the result

✅ Batch API for: overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test gen, bulk non-blocking processing

💡 It's a LATENCY decision, not just a cost decision.
💡 Cost savings are worthless if developers wait 24 hours for a PR check.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Use a higher-tier model with a larger context window to fix attention dilution'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Context window SIZE ≠ attention QUALITY.

A 200K context window can still suffer 'lost in the middle.'
The model can miss findings from middle sections regardless of window size.

✅ CORRECT approaches:
• Split into focused per-file passes + cross-file integration pass
• Place key findings SUMMARY at the BEGINNING of aggregated inputs
• Use explicit section headers to organize long inputs
• Spawn subagents for parallel focused analysis

💡 Bigger window = more room. It does NOT fix how attention is distributed.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Return empty results on subagent failure — graceful degradation'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG. Silent suppression is an anti-pattern.

Empty result = coordinator CANNOT distinguish between:
• 'No matches found' (valid, legitimate empty result)
• 'Agent failed' (error requiring recovery)

This prevents any recovery and risks incomplete outputs presented as complete.

✅ CORRECT: Return structured error context
{ failure_type, attempted_query, partial_results, potential_alternatives }

💡 The coordinator needs the distinction to decide:
   retry? try alternative source? annotate as gap in synthesis?
💡 What the coordinator cannot see, it cannot recover from.

❌ WRONG.

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is USER-LEVEL — it lives on the lead's machine only.
New team members NEVER receive these conventions.
This file is NOT version-controlled, NOT sharable.

✅ CORRECT: .claude/CLAUDE.md at project root, committed to git.
Automatically available to everyone who clones the repository.

⚠️ EXAM FAVORITE: 'New developer joins, conventions not applied'
→ Root cause: conventions stored at user-level instead of project-level

Diagnose with /memory command: shows which files are actually loaded.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Parse assistant text for "task complete" to terminate an agentic loop'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Natural language parsing is UNRELIABLE for loop termination.
Model might phrase completion differently, or produce this text mid-task.

✅ CORRECT: Check stop_reason
• stop_reason === 'tool_use' → execute tool, append result, CONTINUE loop
• stop_reason === 'end_turn' → terminate, return response to user

⚠️ Iteration caps = safety net ONLY (not the primary termination mechanism)

💡 stop_reason is the only reliable, deterministic loop control signal.
💡 It cannot be mimicked by model output. It IS the API contract.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Use sentiment analysis to detect when to escalate to a human'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Frustration ≠ case complexity.

A customer can be furious about a simple item replacement — no escalation needed.
A complex policy exception customer might be perfectly calm — escalation needed.

✅ CORRECT escalation triggers:
• Customer EXPLICITLY requests a human → immediate escalation
• Policy gap (ambiguous/silent on specific request)
• Agent cannot make meaningful progress

For frustration without explicit escalation request:
→ Acknowledge → propose concrete resolution
→ Escalate ONLY if customer REITERATES the human request

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Blindly use --resume to restart a crashed pipeline'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

--resume on a crashed session = stale, unreliable tool results.
Agent may re-process completed docs or skip partially processed ones.

✅ CORRECT:
1. Extract completed work to structured JSON CHECKPOINT
   { complete: [...], partial: [{id, sections_done}], pending: [...] }
2. Start a FRESH session
3. INJECT checkpoint at top of the prompt
→ Agent knows exactly where to resume from

fork_session = divergent exploration from shared baseline
--resume = continue a valid prior session
Checkpoint + fresh session = crash recovery

💡 Stale tool results are untrustworthy. Always checkpoint before they become needed.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Prose summaries passed between agents preserve source attribution'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Prose summaries COMPRESS metadata:
• URLs, page numbers, publication dates collapse into sentences
• Under token pressure, models drop metadata from prose
• Once lost, attribution cannot be reconstructed downstream

✅ CORRECT structural approach:
1. Assign citation_id at SOURCE DISCOVERY level
2. Synthesis writes narrative with inline [src_001] references
3. Pass SEPARATE structured citation index:
   { id, url, source_name, date, key_quote }

💡 Separate content from metadata STRUCTURALLY.
💡 Never rely on prose to preserve both simultaneously.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'tool_choice: "any" forces the model to call a specific named tool'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

"any" means the model MUST call SOME tool — but it CHOOSES WHICH.

Correct distinctions:
• "auto" → model decides: call a tool OR return text (default)
• "any" → model MUST call A tool; picks which one itself
• {"type":"tool","name":"X"} → model MUST call THIS SPECIFIC NAMED TOOL

When to use each:
• "auto" → most cases
• "any" → need guaranteed structured output; model picks the right schema
• Forced → enforcing prerequisite execution order

💡 "any" ≠ forced. "any" guarantees a tool call. Forced guarantees WHICH tool.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Add more detailed system prompt instructions to fix tool selection errors'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG as a first step.

Root cause: tool DESCRIPTIONS are the primary selection mechanism.
Minimal/overlapping descriptions = model guesses, not reads instructions.
Adding system prompt text doesn't fix the root cause.

✅ CORRECT first step: EXPAND AND CLARIFY TOOL DESCRIPTIONS
→ Include input formats, example queries, edge cases
→ Define explicit NEGATIVE BOUNDARIES vs similar tools
   ('archive_file: Do NOT use for compliance files — use archive_for_compliance')
→ Rename to eliminate functional overlap
→ Then add system prompt context IF descriptions alone aren't sufficient

💡 Fix descriptions first. Routing classifiers = over-engineering before basics are right.

trap.fr: ⚠️ TRAP: 'Subagents share memory and can access each other's results'
trap.ba:
❌ WRONG.

Subagents do NOT share memory between invocations.
Each Task tool invocation creates a fresh, fully isolated context.

There is NO:
• Shared state between subagents
• Automatic history propagation from coordinator to subagents
• Memory that persists across Task tool invocations

✅ CORRECT:
• Pass ALL required information explicitly in each subagent's prompt
• Coordinator holds state and injects relevant pieces into each subagent's context
• Use structured state files (scratchpad.md, agent-state/*.json) for persistence

💡 Every subagent starts fresh. Architect for it explicitly — don't work around it.
